1	# The Financial Half: What Makes a Causal-Chain Tool Defensible to a Finance Reviewer
2	
3	*Independent review, written without reading the existing implementation. Perspective: macro/event-driven PM + risk quant.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 0. The one idea the whole finance layer hangs on
8	
9	A causal-chain tool that says "Hormuz opens → oil falls 12% → short USO" is worthless, and a finance-literate reviewer will say so in thirty seconds. The market already knows Hormuz might open. **The conditional move is not the edge. The disagreement is the edge.**
10	
11	Formally, if the market prices scenario *s* with probability *qₛ* and you price it *pₛ*, and the asset is worth *Sₛ* in scenario *s*, then today's price is roughly *S₀ = Σ qₛ Sₛ*, your fair value is *S\* = Σ pₛ Sₛ*, and your expected repricing is
12	
13	> **Edge = S\* − S₀ = Σₛ (pₛ − qₛ) · Sₛ**
14	
15	Set *p = q* and the edge is exactly zero no matter how violent the event. Everything below is scaffolding around that identity. If the tool can't display it, it's a narrative generator wearing a finance costume.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 1. Bridging events to prices
20	
21	### 1a. Scenario-conditional return distributions
22	
23	Each leaf of the chain needs, per instrument: a **conditional return distribution**, not a point. The minimum viable object is a three-point elicitation — *(r_low, r_base, r_high)* interpreted as the 5th/50th/95th percentiles — converted to a Gaussian (in log space) via **σ = (r_high − r_low) / 3.29** and μ = r_base. That's honest, cheap, and auditable. Two or three numbers per (scenario, asset) pair is the entire data model.
24	
25	### 1b. Getting *q* — what's already priced in — cheaply
26	
27	Four ladders, in increasing cost:
28	
29	1. **Prediction markets.** Polymarket's Gamma API (`https://gamma-api.polymarket.com/markets`) and CLOB price history, and Kalshi's read endpoints, are public and keyless ([Polymarket docs](https://docs.polymarket.com/quickstart/reference/endpoints), [Kalshi docs](https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/quick_start_market_data)). Mid-price ≈ implied probability. Calibration is genuinely good — Polymarket's aggregate Brier around 0.19 is superforecaster-class ([Keyrock](https://keyrock.com/knowledge-hub/prediction-market-accuracy-brier-scores/)) — but adjust for spread, fees, and the cost of capital on long-dated contracts (a 0.95 resolving in 9 months is not a 95% belief).
30	2. **Option-implied.** Breeden–Litzenberger: the risk-neutral density is *q(K) = e^{rT} ∂²C/∂K²*, and the digital probability is *P_Q(S_T > K) = −e^{rT} ∂C/∂K* ([overview](https://metricgate.com/docs/option-implied-distribution/), [BSIC](https://bsic.it/risk-neutral-density-estimation-from-option-prices/)). **Do not fit a spline surface.** The 20-line version: a call spread's normalized price, *e^{rT}(C(K₁) − C(K₂))/(K₂ − K₁)*, brackets *P_Q(S_T > K)* between K₁ and K₂. That's one free option chain and arithmetic.
31	3. **Straddle implied move.** For the expiry that spans the event, the ATM straddle price over spot is, to first order, the market's **expected absolute move** *E|ΔS|/S*; the one-sigma move is ≈1.25× that (traders' shorthand is "85% of the straddle," [Options Hawk](https://optionshawk.com/calculating-expected-moves-using-options/), [MenthorQ](https://menthorq.com/guide/from-straddle-price-to-expected-move/)). Isolate the event by differencing variances across two expiries: *σ²_event ≈ T₂σ₂² − T₁σ₁²*. Concave pre-event IV curves are the market literally pricing a bimodal outcome ([Review of Finance](https://academic.oup.com/rof/article/29/4/963/8079062)).
32	4. **Futures curves / rate-path arithmetic.** CME FedWatch is just 100 − ZQ price, day-weighted around the meeting date, assuming 25bp increments ([CME methodology](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/2023/understanding-the-cme-group-fedwatch-tool-methodology.html)). Reimplementable in an afternoon; same logic applies to the oil futures curve (backwardation steepness = priced supply anxiety).
33	
34	**Label these risk-neutral, always.** Option- and futures-implied probabilities are *Q*-measure, inflated in the crash tail by the variance risk premium. Treating them as beliefs is a real error; showing the number with a "risk-neutral, contains risk premium" badge converts a bug into a credibility signal.
35	
36	### 1c. Magnitudes from literature, not vibes
37	
38	- **Oil.** Short-run supply and demand elasticities are tiny — supply ~0.08, demand ~−0.08 in the Caldara–Cavallo–Iacoviello estimates ([Fed IFDP 1173](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/ifdp/2016/files/ifdp1173.pdf)); Hamilton's survey gives gasoline demand ≈ −0.25 ([Hamilton](https://econweb.ucsd.edu/~jhamilto/understand_oil.pdf)). With ε ≈ 0.1, a 1% supply loss implies ~10% price move — that single number does more work than any LLM guess. Kilian's decomposition matters too: *flow supply* shocks historically moved price less than *flow demand* shocks ([Kilian 2009](http://www.douglaslaxton.org/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/kilian.notalloilprices.paper.pdf)), so a chain resting on "supply disruption → huge price move" is arguing against the base rate and must say why.
39	- **Geopolitics.** The Caldara–Iacoviello GPR index is free, monthly/daily, country-level ([policyuncertainty.com/gpr.html](https://www.policyuncertainty.com/gpr.html), [Fed IFDP 1222](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/ifdp/files/ifdp1222.pdf)). Key nuance to encode: GPR spikes are *not* reliably associated with higher oil prices — when GPR rises and oil falls, that's a demand/macro shock, not an energy shock ([CEPR](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/geopolitical-oil-price-shocks-why-these-shocks-hit-harder), [ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/focus/2024/html/ecb.ebbox202308_02~ed883ebf56.en.html)).
40	- **Analog events.** Standard event-study machinery — estimation window, event window, cumulative abnormal return ([EventStudyTools](https://www.eventstudytools.com/introduction-event-study-methodology)) — is a ~50-line function over free daily bars. "The last 6 comparable episodes: median CAR +7%, range −2% to +19%" is the single most persuasive artifact the tool can produce.
41	- **When there's no data**, say so. Ask for a range, name the reference class, stamp it `LLM-ESTIMATE` or `USER`.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## 2. Scenario tree → payoff distribution
46	
47	**Mixture.** Path probability *pₛ = Π pᵢ* along the chain; then
48	
49	- *E[R] = Σ pₛ μₛ*
50	- *Var[R] = Σ pₛ(σₛ² + μₛ²) − (Σ pₛ μₛ)²* — the between-scenario term is where the interesting risk lives
51	- VaR/CVaR: numeric quantiles of the mixture CDF. Five lines.
52	
53	**Path dependence is where naive tools die.** P(terminal price below stop) ≠ P(stop gets hit). For a driftless process they differ by ~2×. Closed form, with log-barrier *b = ln(Stop/S₀) < 0* and *ν = μ − σ²/2*:
54	
55	> *P(min ≤ b) = Φ((b − νT)/(σ√T)) + e^{2νb/σ²} · Φ((b + νT)/(σ√T))*
56	
57	which collapses to *2Φ(b/(σ√T))* when ν = 0 — the reflection principle ([Brownian first passage](https://almostsuremath.com/2023/04/18/the-maximum-of-brownian-motion-and-the-reflection-principle/)). For **both** a stop and a target there's no tidy closed form: run 1,000 daily GBM paths per scenario with scenario-conditional drift and vol, record first touch. That's ~15 lines and it gives P(stop first), P(target first), P(neither) — exactly the brief's "what events could lead to stop losses/take profits."
58	
59	**Horizon alignment** is the most-skipped, cheapest-to-fix item. Every node needs a date window. Scenarios resolving after the trade horizon must be counted as *unresolved*, and for options they are worth −premium. Right thesis, wrong expiry is the most common real-world way this kind of analysis loses money.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 3. What a tradeable thesis must contain
64	
65	A fixed schema, rendered as a one-page card. Missing fields are visible holes — that's the point.
66	
67	| Field | Note |
68	|---|---|
69	| Instrument & expression | ticker/contract, linear vs option, why |
70	| Direction, entry, size | with reference price and timestamp |
71	| Horizon | must ≥ the catalyst date distribution |
72	| Catalysts | dated, each linked to a chain node |
73	| **What's priced in** | *q* with source URL, vs your *p* |
74	| Invalidation / kill criteria | a *falsifiable* statement, not "if I'm wrong" |
75	| Stop / target | plus P(touch) from §2 |
76	| Key risks | the 3 highest-probability adverse chains |
77	| Monitoring signposts | observables that update node probabilities |
78	
79	**Expression choice is a real analytical output, not a dropdown.** Binary, high-conviction, short-horizon → options: convexity and bounded loss, but you're paying the event premium the straddle told you about. Continuous/uncertain-timing → linear or futures. **Relative value** (crack spreads, tanker-vs-refiner, Brent–WTI) isolates the factor and strips out the beta you have no view on — it's usually the more defensible trade and almost nobody's tool suggests it. **Second-order beneficiaries** are use case 2's entire payload: for Hormuz, VLCC rates, war-risk insurance, refiners, airlines, Gulf-adjacent sovereigns. The magnitudes there are enormous — reported VLCC benchmark spikes to record levels and war-risk premia up ~40× ([Lloyd's List](https://www.lloydslist.com/LL1156586/Gulf-war-risk-premiums-topping-double-digit-millions-of-dollars-per-trip), [Caixin](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-03-07/war-risk-insurance-returns-to-strait-of-hormuz-at-a-price-102420420.html)) — which is exactly why they're usually *already moved* by the time a headline exists. Flag second-order ideas with a "check what's already moved" prompt showing trailing 1M/3M returns.
80	
81	---
82	
83	## 4. Sizing
84	
85	Kelly for a binary: *f\* = p − (1−p)/b*. For a continuous return: *f\* ≈ μ/σ²*.
86	
87	**Full Kelly on LLM-generated probabilities is reckless.** Growth rate is flat near the optimum but turns *negative* past 2f\*, and modest estimation error produces large overbets — MacLean–Thorp–Ziemba is the canonical reference ([Quantitative Finance 2010](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/10.1142/9789811285530_0015), [Ziemba chapter](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/mckinnon/blackouts/StochOptFinanceAndEnergySpringer/Chap1_KellyZiemba.pdf)); half-Kelly retains ~75% of growth with far less drawdown ([Kelly criterion overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_criterion)). With ±15pp probability error bars — realistic for model-elicited beliefs — the sign of the edge can flip.
88	
89	So: **(a)** make the primary sizing rule the practitioner one — *size = risk_budget_$ / (entry − stop)* per unit, with risk budget ≈ 0.5–2% of capital; **(b)** show Kelly as secondary, capped at ¼, and computed at the *pessimistic* end of the probability interval (*p_low*, not *p*); **(c)** show a worst-scenario sizing check: "in your worst leaf, this position loses X% of capital — acceptable?" Three lines of code, and it is what actually gets used.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## 5. Black swans and risk
94	
95	**Reverse stress testing is the brief.** Regulators define it as fixing an adverse outcome and deducing the scenarios that produce it ([OCC 2012-33](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2012/bulletin-2012-33.html), [S&P Global](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/reverse-stress-testing-assessment-tool-risk-managers-regulators)). Applied here: enumerate leaves, filter to those where P&L ≤ stop, rank by probability, and **extract the node common to the worst paths**. "Three chains totalling 14% probability produce 80% of your stop-outs; all three pass through *Iran strikes back*" is a genuinely valuable, cheap-to-compute output that no consumer tool ships.
96	
97	**Stress, don't probability-weight, the true tails.** Assigning 0.3% to something you can't estimate is fake precision. Present a separate unweighted panel: *if this happens, you lose X*. Correlations go to one in a crisis — tail dependence is pervasive across asset classes ([T. Rowe Price / FAJ, "When Diversification Fails"](https://www.troweprice.com/content/dam/ide/articles/pdfs/2018/q4/when-diversification-fails.pdf)) — so don't estimate a covariance matrix from 250 days; use a **crisis-regime toggle** that forces correlation to ~0.8 among risk assets (with the usual gold/USD/oil sign flips) and multiplies vol. Tail hedges cost roughly 1–4% of portfolio value annually as drag and are contested even among professionals ([AQR](https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Insights/White-Papers/AQR-Tail-Risk-Hedging-Contrasting-Put-and-Trend-Strategies.pdf)) — mention as an expression, don't recommend.
98	
99	---
100	
101	## 6. Data realism and legal hygiene
102	
103	**Feasible free:** FRED (keyed, free, reliable — `DCOILBRENTEU`, `VIXCLS`, `DGS10`); Stooq (no key, CSV, good history); yfinance (prices *and option chains* free, but unofficial and brittle — it broke repeatedly after Yahoo's redesign and is "not recommended for production" per [2026 API survey](https://github.com/jeff3388/awesome-financial-data-apis)); Polymarket/Kalshi public endpoints; EIA (free key) for oil flows and inventories; GPR index Excel. **Cache everything to disk on first fetch** — demos die on rate limits.
104	
105	**Everything else is user-entered or model-estimated, and must say so.** Ship a four-value provenance enum on *every number*: `MARKET` (source + timestamp + URL), `HISTORICAL` (method + window), `LLM-ESTIMATE` (unverified), `USER`. Render them differently. Blurring an LLM's "oil +22%" into the same typography as a live Polymarket mid is the single most damaging thing this tool could do.
106	
107	**Legal:** display a persistent "not investment advice / educational / no recommendation" notice; keep output general and impersonal rather than tailored to an individual's circumstances (this is the shape of the publisher's exclusion under the Advisers Act — [analysis](https://natlawreview.com/article/navigating-publishers-exclusion-under-advisers-act)); no order routing, no brokerage links, no performance claims. One modal on first run plus a footer is sufficient and costs nothing.
108	
109	---
110	
111	## 7. Failure modes to design against
112	
113	1. **Conjunction fallacy.** Detailed stories feel more likely and are less likely. Five nodes at 0.8 = 0.33. Display joint path probability at maximum prominence.
114	2. **Base-rate neglect**, worst precisely when the story is good ([outside view](https://gc-bs.org/articles/outer-view-defeating-overconfidence-bias-through-baserate-forecasting/)). Force a reference class on every node.
115	3. **Already priced.** The obvious second-order trade moved last week.
116	4. **Timing.** Options expire; theses don't.
117	5. **Overfit chains.** Tuning node probabilities until the EV looks good is backwards-engineering a conclusion.
118	6. **Sign/regime errors.** Geopolitical risk up + oil down is a *different shock* than geopolitical risk up + oil up.
119	7. **Survivorship in analogs.** You remember the Hormuz scares that moved oil.
120	
121	---
122	
123	## (a) The minimal finance core — 80% of credibility, 20% of effort
124	
125	**Data model.** *Node:* `{id, statement, parent, date_window{start,end}, p_conditional, p_interval[lo,hi], q_market, q_source{venue,url,ts,measure:P|Q}}`. *Impact edge:* `{node_id, ticker, horizon_days, r_low, r_base, r_high, evidence{type: event_study|elasticity|analog|llm, citation}}`. *Position:* `{ticker, direction, entry, stop, target, capital, risk_budget_pct}`.
126	
127	**Six formulas — that's the whole engine:**
128	1. `p_path = Π p_i`, `q_path = Π q_i` (with an explicit "other/neither" sibling so each level sums to 1)
129	2. `σ_s = (r_high − r_low)/3.29`; mixture `E[R] = Σ p_s μ_s`, `Var = Σ p_s(σ_s²+μ_s²) − E[R]²`
130	3. **`Edge = Σ (p_s − q_s)·μ_s`** ← the headline number, next to "market-implied expected move"
131	4. Cross-check: `E|ΔS|/S` vs `straddle/S` from a free option chain
132	5. `P(touch stop)` via the barrier formula per scenario, mixed; both-barrier via 1k-path MC
133	6. `size = min( risk_budget$/(entry−stop), 0.25 × Kelly(p_lo) )`
134	
135	**Plus one report:** reverse stress — worst paths by P&L, cumulative probability, modal node. **Plus one badge:** provenance on every number.
136	
137	## (b) Eight rigor traps, each with a test
138	
139	1. **No priced-in comparison.** *Test:* set every *p* equal to its *q*. Edge must read ≈0. If the tool still says "attractive," it is a hype machine.
140	2. **Risk-neutral laundering.** *Test:* hover an option-derived probability. It must be labelled *Q*-measure / contains risk premium. If a 3% put-implied crash probability is presented as a belief, fail.
141	3. **Terminal vs barrier.** *Test:* driftless scenario, stop at −1σ over the horizon. P(touch) ≈ 32%, P(end below) ≈ 16%. If they're equal, path dependence is missing.
142	4. **Conjunction / normalization.** *Test:* build a 5-deep chain of 0.8s — must display 0.33, not 0.8. Separately, check sibling probabilities at each node sum to 1 (is there an "other" branch?).
143	5. **Horizon misalignment.** *Test:* push the event date past the option expiry. EV must collapse toward −premium, not stay unchanged.
144	6. **Double counting.** *Test:* add "Iran struck" downstream of "Hormuz disrupted," both with an oil impact. The tool must treat the child's impact as *marginal*, not add two full moves.
145	7. **Sizing blow-up.** *Test:* set p = 0.95 with interval [0.5, 0.99]. Kelly must not suggest a near-full-capital bet; the interval must bind, and the risk-budget number must be the default shown.
146	8. **Provenance blur.** *Test:* click any number. It must name source, method, and timestamp. Indistinguishable rendering of market data and model guesses is disqualifying.
147	
148	*Honorable mentions:* unit/sign discipline (`+$10/bbl` vs `+10%`; a short's stop is above entry), and treating two legs of the same factor as diversifying.
149	
150	## (c) What NOT to build
151	
152	- **Portfolio optimizer.** Markowitz over five invented correlations launders noise into false precision.
153	- **Backtester.** You cannot backtest hypothetical chains; there's no sample, and it invites overfitting. Backtest *analog event studies* instead — same credibility, 5% of the work.
154	- **Spline/SVI-fitted risk-neutral densities.** Call spreads get you 90% of the signal.
155	- **Covariance/factor model, copulas, EVT.** Use a crisis-regime toggle.
156	- **Live streaming data, broker integration, alerts.** Daily closes cached to disk.
157	- **Exotic option pricing.** Black-Scholes closed form and nothing more.
158	- **Probability calibration training for the LLM.** Out of scope; instead, always show the market's number beside the model's and let the disagreement be the product.

# The Financial Half: What Makes a Causal-Chain Tool Defensible to a Finance Reviewer

*Independent review, written without reading the existing implementation. Perspective: macro/event-driven PM + risk quant.*

---

## 0. The one idea the whole finance layer hangs on

A causal-chain tool that says "Hormuz opens → oil falls 12% → short USO" is worthless, and a finance-literate reviewer will say so in thirty seconds. The market already knows Hormuz might open. **The conditional move is not the edge. The disagreement is the edge.**

Formally, if the market prices scenario *s* with probability *qₛ* and you price it *pₛ*, and the asset is worth *Sₛ* in scenario *s*, then today's price is roughly *S₀ = Σ qₛ Sₛ*, your fair value is *S\* = Σ pₛ Sₛ*, and your expected repricing is

> **Edge = S\* − S₀ = Σₛ (pₛ − qₛ) · Sₛ**

Set *p = q* and the edge is exactly zero no matter how violent the event. Everything below is scaffolding around that identity. If the tool can't display it, it's a narrative generator wearing a finance costume.

---

## 1. Bridging events to prices

### 1a. Scenario-conditional return distributions

Each leaf of the chain needs, per instrument: a **conditional return distribution**, not a point. The minimum viable object is a three-point elicitation — *(r_low, r_base, r_high)* interpreted as the 5th/50th/95th percentiles — converted to a Gaussian (in log space) via **σ = (r_high − r_low) / 3.29** and μ = r_base. That's honest, cheap, and auditable. Two or three numbers per (scenario, asset) pair is the entire data model.

### 1b. Getting *q* — what's already priced in — cheaply

Four ladders, in increasing cost:

1. **Prediction markets.** Polymarket's Gamma API (`https://gamma-api.polymarket.com/markets`) and CLOB price history, and Kalshi's read endpoints, are public and keyless ([Polymarket docs](https://docs.polymarket.com/quickstart/reference/endpoints), [Kalshi docs](https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/quick_start_market_data)). Mid-price ≈ implied probability. Calibration is genuinely good — Polymarket's aggregate Brier around 0.19 is superforecaster-class ([Keyrock](https://keyrock.com/knowledge-hub/prediction-market-accuracy-brier-scores/)) — but adjust for spread, fees, and the cost of capital on long-dated contracts (a 0.95 resolving in 9 months is not a 95% belief).
2. **Option-implied.** Breeden–Litzenberger: the risk-neutral density is *q(K) = e^{rT} ∂²C/∂K²*, and the digital probability is *P_Q(S_T > K) = −e^{rT} ∂C/∂K* ([overview](https://metricgate.com/docs/option-implied-distribution/), [BSIC](https://bsic.it/risk-neutral-density-estimation-from-option-prices/)). **Do not fit a spline surface.** The 20-line version: a call spread's normalized price, *e^{rT}(C(K₁) − C(K₂))/(K₂ − K₁)*, brackets *P_Q(S_T > K)* between K₁ and K₂. That's one free option chain and arithmetic.
3. **Straddle implied move.** For the expiry that spans the event, the ATM straddle price over spot is, to first order, the market's **expected absolute move** *E|ΔS|/S*; the one-sigma move is ≈1.25× that (traders' shorthand is "85% of the straddle," [Options Hawk](https://optionshawk.com/calculating-expected-moves-using-options/), [MenthorQ](https://menthorq.com/guide/from-straddle-price-to-expected-move/)). Isolate the event by differencing variances across two expiries: *σ²_event ≈ T₂σ₂² − T₁σ₁²*. Concave pre-event IV curves are the market literally pricing a bimodal outcome ([Review of Finance](https://academic.oup.com/rof/article/29/4/963/8079062)).
4. **Futures curves / rate-path arithmetic.** CME FedWatch is just 100 − ZQ price, day-weighted around the meeting date, assuming 25bp increments ([CME methodology](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/2023/understanding-the-cme-group-fedwatch-tool-methodology.html)). Reimplementable in an afternoon; same logic applies to the oil futures curve (backwardation steepness = priced supply anxiety).

**Label these risk-neutral, always.** Option- and futures-implied probabilities are *Q*-measure, inflated in the crash tail by the variance risk premium. Treating them as beliefs is a real error; showing the number with a "risk-neutral, contains risk premium" badge converts a bug into a credibility signal.

### 1c. Magnitudes from literature, not vibes

- **Oil.** Short-run supply and demand elasticities are tiny — supply ~0.08, demand ~−0.08 in the Caldara–Cavallo–Iacoviello estimates ([Fed IFDP 1173](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/ifdp/2016/files/ifdp1173.pdf)); Hamilton's survey gives gasoline demand ≈ −0.25 ([Hamilton](https://econweb.ucsd.edu/~jhamilto/understand_oil.pdf)). With ε ≈ 0.1, a 1% supply loss implies ~10% price move — that single number does more work than any LLM guess. Kilian's decomposition matters too: *flow supply* shocks historically moved price less than *flow demand* shocks ([Kilian 2009](http://www.douglaslaxton.org/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/kilian.notalloilprices.paper.pdf)), so a chain resting on "supply disruption → huge price move" is arguing against the base rate and must say why.
- **Geopolitics.** The Caldara–Iacoviello GPR index is free, monthly/daily, country-level ([policyuncertainty.com/gpr.html](https://www.policyuncertainty.com/gpr.html), [Fed IFDP 1222](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/ifdp/files/ifdp1222.pdf)). Key nuance to encode: GPR spikes are *not* reliably associated with higher oil prices — when GPR rises and oil falls, that's a demand/macro shock, not an energy shock ([CEPR](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/geopolitical-oil-price-shocks-why-these-shocks-hit-harder), [ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/focus/2024/html/ecb.ebbox202308_02~ed883ebf56.en.html)).
- **Analog events.** Standard event-study machinery — estimation window, event window, cumulative abnormal return ([EventStudyTools](https://www.eventstudytools.com/introduction-event-study-methodology)) — is a ~50-line function over free daily bars. "The last 6 comparable episodes: median CAR +7%, range −2% to +19%" is the single most persuasive artifact the tool can produce.
- **When there's no data**, say so. Ask for a range, name the reference class, stamp it `LLM-ESTIMATE` or `USER`.

---

## 2. Scenario tree → payoff distribution

**Mixture.** Path probability *pₛ = Π pᵢ* along the chain; then

- *E[R] = Σ pₛ μₛ*
- *Var[R] = Σ pₛ(σₛ² + μₛ²) − (Σ pₛ μₛ)²* — the between-scenario term is where the interesting risk lives
- VaR/CVaR: numeric quantiles of the mixture CDF. Five lines.

**Path dependence is where naive tools die.** P(terminal price below stop) ≠ P(stop gets hit). For a driftless process they differ by ~2×. Closed form, with log-barrier *b = ln(Stop/S₀) < 0* and *ν = μ − σ²/2*:

> *P(min ≤ b) = Φ((b − νT)/(σ√T)) + e^{2νb/σ²} · Φ((b + νT)/(σ√T))*

which collapses to *2Φ(b/(σ√T))* when ν = 0 — the reflection principle ([Brownian first passage](https://almostsuremath.com/2023/04/18/the-maximum-of-brownian-motion-and-the-reflection-principle/)). For **both** a stop and a target there's no tidy closed form: run 1,000 daily GBM paths per scenario with scenario-conditional drift and vol, record first touch. That's ~15 lines and it gives P(stop first), P(target first), P(neither) — exactly the brief's "what events could lead to stop losses/take profits."

**Horizon alignment** is the most-skipped, cheapest-to-fix item. Every node needs a date window. Scenarios resolving after the trade horizon must be counted as *unresolved*, and for options they are worth −premium. Right thesis, wrong expiry is the most common real-world way this kind of analysis loses money.

---

## 3. What a tradeable thesis must contain

A fixed schema, rendered as a one-page card. Missing fields are visible holes — that's the point.

| Field | Note |
|---|---|
| Instrument & expression | ticker/contract, linear vs option, why |
| Direction, entry, size | with reference price and timestamp |
| Horizon | must ≥ the catalyst date distribution |
| Catalysts | dated, each linked to a chain node |
| **What's priced in** | *q* with source URL, vs your *p* |
| Invalidation / kill criteria | a *falsifiable* statement, not "if I'm wrong" |
| Stop / target | plus P(touch) from §2 |
| Key risks | the 3 highest-probability adverse chains |
| Monitoring signposts | observables that update node probabilities |

**Expression choice is a real analytical output, not a dropdown.** Binary, high-conviction, short-horizon → options: convexity and bounded loss, but you're paying the event premium the straddle told you about. Continuous/uncertain-timing → linear or futures. **Relative value** (crack spreads, tanker-vs-refiner, Brent–WTI) isolates the factor and strips out the beta you have no view on — it's usually the more defensible trade and almost nobody's tool suggests it. **Second-order beneficiaries** are use case 2's entire payload: for Hormuz, VLCC rates, war-risk insurance, refiners, airlines, Gulf-adjacent sovereigns. The magnitudes there are enormous — reported VLCC benchmark spikes to record levels and war-risk premia up ~40× ([Lloyd's List](https://www.lloydslist.com/LL1156586/Gulf-war-risk-premiums-topping-double-digit-millions-of-dollars-per-trip), [Caixin](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-03-07/war-risk-insurance-returns-to-strait-of-hormuz-at-a-price-102420420.html)) — which is exactly why they're usually *already moved* by the time a headline exists. Flag second-order ideas with a "check what's already moved" prompt showing trailing 1M/3M returns.

---

## 4. Sizing

Kelly for a binary: *f\* = p − (1−p)/b*. For a continuous return: *f\* ≈ μ/σ²*.

**Full Kelly on LLM-generated probabilities is reckless.** Growth rate is flat near the optimum but turns *negative* past 2f\*, and modest estimation error produces large overbets — MacLean–Thorp–Ziemba is the canonical reference ([Quantitative Finance 2010](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/10.1142/9789811285530_0015), [Ziemba chapter](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/mckinnon/blackouts/StochOptFinanceAndEnergySpringer/Chap1_KellyZiemba.pdf)); half-Kelly retains ~75% of growth with far less drawdown ([Kelly criterion overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_criterion)). With ±15pp probability error bars — realistic for model-elicited beliefs — the sign of the edge can flip.

So: **(a)** make the primary sizing rule the practitioner one — *size = risk_budget_$ / (entry − stop)* per unit, with risk budget ≈ 0.5–2% of capital; **(b)** show Kelly as secondary, capped at ¼, and computed at the *pessimistic* end of the probability interval (*p_low*, not *p*); **(c)** show a worst-scenario sizing check: "in your worst leaf, this position loses X% of capital — acceptable?" Three lines of code, and it is what actually gets used.

---

## 5. Black swans and risk

**Reverse stress testing is the brief.** Regulators define it as fixing an adverse outcome and deducing the scenarios that produce it ([OCC 2012-33](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2012/bulletin-2012-33.html), [S&P Global](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/reverse-stress-testing-assessment-tool-risk-managers-regulators)). Applied here: enumerate leaves, filter to those where P&L ≤ stop, rank by probability, and **extract the node common to the worst paths**. "Three chains totalling 14% probability produce 80% of your stop-outs; all three pass through *Iran strikes back*" is a genuinely valuable, cheap-to-compute output that no consumer tool ships.

**Stress, don't probability-weight, the true tails.** Assigning 0.3% to something you can't estimate is fake precision. Present a separate unweighted panel: *if this happens, you lose X*. Correlations go to one in a crisis — tail dependence is pervasive across asset classes ([T. Rowe Price / FAJ, "When Diversification Fails"](https://www.troweprice.com/content/dam/ide/articles/pdfs/2018/q4/when-diversification-fails.pdf)) — so don't estimate a covariance matrix from 250 days; use a **crisis-regime toggle** that forces correlation to ~0.8 among risk assets (with the usual gold/USD/oil sign flips) and multiplies vol. Tail hedges cost roughly 1–4% of portfolio value annually as drag and are contested even among professionals ([AQR](https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Insights/White-Papers/AQR-Tail-Risk-Hedging-Contrasting-Put-and-Trend-Strategies.pdf)) — mention as an expression, don't recommend.

---

## 6. Data realism and legal hygiene

**Feasible free:** FRED (keyed, free, reliable — `DCOILBRENTEU`, `VIXCLS`, `DGS10`); Stooq (no key, CSV, good history); yfinance (prices *and option chains* free, but unofficial and brittle — it broke repeatedly after Yahoo's redesign and is "not recommended for production" per [2026 API survey](https://github.com/jeff3388/awesome-financial-data-apis)); Polymarket/Kalshi public endpoints; EIA (free key) for oil flows and inventories; GPR index Excel. **Cache everything to disk on first fetch** — demos die on rate limits.

**Everything else is user-entered or model-estimated, and must say so.** Ship a four-value provenance enum on *every number*: `MARKET` (source + timestamp + URL), `HISTORICAL` (method + window), `LLM-ESTIMATE` (unverified), `USER`. Render them differently. Blurring an LLM's "oil +22%" into the same typography as a live Polymarket mid is the single most damaging thing this tool could do.

**Legal:** display a persistent "not investment advice / educational / no recommendation" notice; keep output general and impersonal rather than tailored to an individual's circumstances (this is the shape of the publisher's exclusion under the Advisers Act — [analysis](https://natlawreview.com/article/navigating-publishers-exclusion-under-advisers-act)); no order routing, no brokerage links, no performance claims. One modal on first run plus a footer is sufficient and costs nothing.

---

## 7. Failure modes to design against

1. **Conjunction fallacy.** Detailed stories feel more likely and are less likely. Five nodes at 0.8 = 0.33. Display joint path probability at maximum prominence.
2. **Base-rate neglect**, worst precisely when the story is good ([outside view](https://gc-bs.org/articles/outer-view-defeating-overconfidence-bias-through-baserate-forecasting/)). Force a reference class on every node.
3. **Already priced.** The obvious second-order trade moved last week.
4. **Timing.** Options expire; theses don't.
5. **Overfit chains.** Tuning node probabilities until the EV looks good is backwards-engineering a conclusion.
6. **Sign/regime errors.** Geopolitical risk up + oil down is a *different shock* than geopolitical risk up + oil up.
7. **Survivorship in analogs.** You remember the Hormuz scares that moved oil.

---

## (a) The minimal finance core — 80% of credibility, 20% of effort

**Data model.** *Node:* `{id, statement, parent, date_window{start,end}, p_conditional, p_interval[lo,hi], q_market, q_source{venue,url,ts,measure:P|Q}}`. *Impact edge:* `{node_id, ticker, horizon_days, r_low, r_base, r_high, evidence{type: event_study|elasticity|analog|llm, citation}}`. *Position:* `{ticker, direction, entry, stop, target, capital, risk_budget_pct}`.

2. `σ_s = (r_high − r_low)/3.29`; mixture `E[R] = Σ p_s μ_s`, `Var = Σ p_s(σ_s²+μ_s²) − E[R]²`
3. **`Edge = Σ (p_s − q_s)·μ_s`** ← the headline number, next to "market-implied expected move"
4. Cross-check: `E|ΔS|/S` vs `straddle/S` from a free option chain
5. `P(touch stop)` via the barrier formula per scenario, mixed; both-barrier via 1k-path MC
6. `size = min( risk_budget$/(entry−stop), 0.25 × Kelly(p_lo) )`

**Plus one report:** reverse stress — worst paths by P&L, cumulative probability, modal node. **Plus one badge:** provenance on every number.

## (b) Eight rigor traps, each with a test

2. **Risk-neutral laundering.** *Test:* hover an option-derived probability. It must be labelled *Q*-measure / contains risk premium. If a 3% put-implied crash probability is presented as a belief, fail.
3. **Terminal vs barrier.** *Test:* driftless scenario, stop at −1σ over the horizon. P(touch) ≈ 32%, P(end below) ≈ 16%. If they're equal, path dependence is missing.
4. **Conjunction / normalization.** *Test:* build a 5-deep chain of 0.8s — must display 0.33, not 0.8. Separately, check sibling probabilities at each node sum to 1 (is there an "other" branch?).
5. **Horizon misalignment.** *Test:* push the event date past the option expiry. EV must collapse toward −premium, not stay unchanged.
6. **Double counting.** *Test:* add "Iran struck" downstream of "Hormuz disrupted," both with an oil impact. The tool must treat the child's impact as *marginal*, not add two full moves.
7. **Sizing blow-up.** *Test:* set p = 0.95 with interval [0.5, 0.99]. Kelly must not suggest a near-full-capital bet; the interval must bind, and the risk-budget number must be the default shown.

1	# A small quantitative alternative, worked end to end
2	
3	**Status:** design experiment proposed for review; no product code changed. Every number below is invented for arithmetic demonstration, not a Hormuz forecast, a researched parameter, or a real market quote. Decimal precision is retained to let a reviewer reproduce the arithmetic; the product can round its display.
4	
5	## What this experiment should settle
6	
7	Can a small explicit causal model demonstrate the assignment's two use cases, immediate branching, and a financially meaningful thesis more clearly than the current temporal simulator?
8	
9	The candidate uses four binary variables with fixed meanings. It has no sampled parameter distribution, daily noise process, implicit expiry of an assumption, or multiplied path score. It remains a **subjective causal hypothesis**. Correct arithmetic does not validate its assumptions.
10	
11	## Define the claims and the relationships
12	
13	| Variable | Claim | Role |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| H | The strait reopens on Monday under the chosen transit criterion | Historical event within the scenario |
16	| S | A specified military strike occurs on Tuesday | Additional event |
17	| F | Effective shipping flow exceeds the chosen threshold at the end of the first week | Continuing state, assessed at a date |
18	| B | The named Brent benchmark closes below the chosen threshold at the end of the second week | Financial outcome |
19	
20	Proposed graph: `H → F ← S`, then `F → B`.
21	
22	The mechanism hypothesis is that reopening enables flow recovery, a strike can hinder it, and recovered flow makes a lower price more likely. This is intentionally incomplete: demand, inventories, supply policy, and risk premia are held in background assumptions. If a strike affects price through an additional risk-premium channel, add `S → B` and the corresponding conditional table; do not pretend the flow channel captures it. If the chance of a strike depends on reopening, model that dependency instead of assuming independence.
23	
24	For this arithmetic example only, H and S are independent roots with `P(H)=0.35` and `P(S)=0.20`. That independence is an assumption to challenge, not a property of geopolitical events.
25	
26	## Write the local assumptions explicitly
27	
28	The flow table means the chance that F is true for each combination of its two parents:
29	
30	| H: reopened | S: strike | P(F=true given H,S) |
31	|---|---|---:|
32	| false | false | 0.10 |
33	| false | true | 0.05 |
34	| true | false | 0.80 |
35	| true | true | 0.25 |
36	
37	The last row is the assignment's important interaction. Reopening and then suffering a strike is not the same scenario as reopening with no strike. No additive-strength approximation is required to express that distinction.
38	
39	The financial table is `P(B=true | F=false)=0.20` and `P(B=true | F=true)=0.70`. These are subjective conditional probabilities under the proposed model. Interpreting them causally requires the stated parent structure to be adequate for the intended intervention; an observational table alone does not supply that warrant.
40	
41	The joint probability assigned to one complete state is:
42	
43	`P(H=h,S=s,F=f,B=b) = P(H=h) × P(S=s) × P(F=f | H=h,S=s) × P(B=b | F=f)`.
44	
45	There are only sixteen complete states. Summing their probabilities computes the requested outcome without simulation error. This is the standard factorization of a Bayesian network; the causal interpretation is the additional modeling assumption. [CMU course notes](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15281/coursenotes/bayesnets/).
46	
47	## Explore, then change one event
48	
49	In the opening scenario, the user supposes H is true. The model replaces H's root distribution with that fixed value, leaving the remaining mechanisms unchanged. It does not claim the user can physically control the strait. This is a hypothetical intervention under a declared model. [Pearl, intervention semantics](https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/BOOK-2K/ch3-3.pdf).
50	
51	Then:
52	
53	`P(F | do(H=true)) = 0.80 × 0.80 + 0.20 × 0.25 = 0.69`.
54	
55	`P(B | do(H=true)) = 0.69 × 0.70 + 0.31 × 0.20 = 0.545`.
56	
57	Now create a branch supposing S is also true:
58	
59	`P(F | do(H=true), do(S=true)) = 0.25`.
60	
61	`P(B | do(H=true), do(S=true)) = 0.25 × 0.70 + 0.75 × 0.20 = 0.325`.
62	
63	The branch lowers the model-implied chance of B by **22 percentage points**. The difference is explained by two named local tables. Monday's reopening remains true; Tuesday's strike changes the chance of Friday's flow recovery. No historical event has to be retracted.
64	
65	The UI can say:
66	
67	> Under these assumptions, a strike after reopening lowers the chance of the Brent threshold being met from 55% to 33%. The change runs through reduced shipping recovery. A direct effect on the risk premium is not modeled.
68	
69	The mechanism's source appears separately from the table's owner and rationale. A source documenting the importance of shipping does not certify the numbers 0.80 or 0.25.
70	
71	## Verify without a path product
72	
73	To test whether reopening helps reach B, compare the defined intervention with its explicit alternative:
74	
75	`P(F | do(H=false)) = 0.80 × 0.10 + 0.20 × 0.05 = 0.09`.
76	
77	`P(B | do(H=false)) = 0.09 × 0.70 + 0.91 × 0.20 = 0.245`.
78	
79	The modeled difference between reopening and not reopening is `0.545 − 0.245 = 0.30`. This answers a precise question under assumptions. It does not show that reopening alone is sufficient for B, prove the graph true, or establish a trade's profitability. “No reopening” can bundle physically different situations; the real-world interpretation is only as well-defined as this binary scenario distinction.
80	
81	A useful Verify verdict is therefore:
82	
83	> This model supports a downward-price mechanism, conditional on shipping recovery. The conclusion weakens substantially under renewed strikes. It remains sensitive to omitted demand and risk-premium mechanisms.
84	
85	A graph search that finds no supported route should report its scope: “No supported chain found within this map and search budget.” It should not claim no causal relationship can exist.
86	
87	## Turn the scenario into a financially valid question
88	
89	Suppose, for illustration, that a matching binary contract pays $1 when B is true and $0 otherwise. A hypothetical executable YES ask is $0.40 and per-unit costs are $0.02.
90	
91	Before H happens, the model's **unconditional** probability is calculated below. Here H has no parents, and the declared model makes `P(B | H)` equal to `P(B | do(H))`. That equality must not be assumed in an arbitrary causal graph.
92	
93	`P(B) = 0.35 × 0.545 + 0.65 × 0.245 = 0.35`.
94	
95	The expected unit payout is $0.35. For a position held to resolution, expected net profit per unit is:
96	
97	`0.35 − 0.40 − 0.02 = −$0.07`.
98	
99	Subtracting the current quote from the opening-scenario probability would instead suggest `0.545 − 0.40 − 0.02 = +$0.125`. That calculation answers a different question: a trade evaluated as though the opening were already given at an unchanged purchase price. It is not the pre-event expected payoff.
100	
101	The honest conclusion is **no positive expected profit at this entry price under this model**. With these flat costs, the break-even probability is `0.40 + 0.02 = 0.42`; at a probability of 0.35, the break-even maximum ask is `$0.35 − $0.02 = $0.33`. Fees that depend on price or winnings require their actual formula. Alternatively, the user can define an entry rule after observing reopening, but the product must then use the quote available at that entry time. It cannot assume the old quote survives the news. This illustration omits quote movement before fill, settlement/counterparty risk, and capital/opportunity cost; it is not an executable trade assessment.
102	
103	For ordinary assets, replace the binary payout with an explicit scenario price and a specified position. A probability of crossing a threshold does not define returns within each outcome, margin needs, maximum drawdown, or a probability of ruin. Leave those outputs absent until their required inputs exist.
104	
105	## Represent uncertainty without manufacturing a distribution
106	
107	Add named alternative assumptions only where they matter. For example:
108	
109	| Assumption set | P(F | H=true,S=false) | P(F | H=true,S=true) | P(B | do(H=true)) |
110	|---|---:|---:|---:|
111	| Fragile recovery | 0.60 | 0.10 | 0.45 |
112	| Central illustration | 0.80 | 0.25 | 0.545 |
113	| Resilient recovery | 0.90 | 0.40 | 0.60 |
114	
115	Other inputs remain fixed for this exercise. The 45–60% span is an **envelope over three tested assumptions**, not an 80% probability interval, not a bound over all plausible models, and not evidence that the true probability lies inside it. Adding the direct risk-premium channel would be a structural sensitivity case.
116	
117	Do not blindly combine all low inputs for a low case and all high inputs for a high case. Negative effects and interactions can make that ordering wrong. Evaluate each specified case and report what was actually tested.
118	
119	This lets a user ask “does my decision survive these alternatives?” without pretending the application knows a probability distribution over all its own errors.
120	
121	## Smallest implementation boundary
122	
123	- Keep the existing immutable graph, branch history, Inspector, source records, generated browser types, and keyless replay idea.
124	- A numerical claim carries its parent set, a complete local conditional table, and a parameter owner/rationale. A claim may remain unquantified.
125	- A model defines a bounded collection of dated binary claims. Numerical dependencies must be closed: an unknown input prevents that output from being calculated.
126	- For a small cap, compute by exact enumeration. Count nodes after any explicit time expansion. If the cap is exceeded, decline the numerical calculation or ask for a smaller focus; do not silently switch semantics.
127	- A scenario edit fixes a specific dated claim. Distinguish this from learning that it occurred. An observation query can be added by exact conditioning once its interface and tests are ready.
128	- Conditional tables do not identify individual-level counterfactuals. Do not claim to know what the same realized world would have done differently without a structural model of its shared disturbances.
129	- Keep named sensitivity cases as complete explicit model variants. Do not turn their counts into probabilities or average them without a justified weighting rule.
130	- Store the model/schema version and the branch in the exported thesis. A later mathematical change should not silently rewrite the meaning of an older artifact.
131	
132	This is a candidate to test, not a demand for a framework supporting every model class. The main tradeoff is elicitation burden: four understandable numbers can be better than two obscure log-odds pushes, but they remain four unsupported numbers if nobody can defend them. If the example cannot justify its parameters, keep the mechanism and show scenario consequences without a numeric probability. That is a valid result of the design experiment.
133	
134	## Acceptance tests before adoption
135	
136	1. Reproduce every calculation above with an independent small enumerator or hand oracle.
137	2. Verify total probability is one and impossible events remain zero.
138	3. In a shared-cause example, distinguish observing an event from intervening on it; reproduce Bayes' rule numerically.
139	4. In an interaction table, preserve the joint-parent row rather than synthesizing it from independent pushes.
140	5. Changing a root assumption leaves unrelated claims unchanged.
141	6. Monday's reopening and Tuesday's strike can both occur without contradiction.
142	7. A missing conditional row or an unquantified parent yields an explicit incomplete result.
143	8. Export the exact branch and assumption set currently displayed.
144	9. Use the unconditional belief for a pre-event binary expected-payoff calculation; use a post-event quote for a post-event entry rule.
145	10. Have a reviewer explain the before/after thesis and identify which inputs are evidence versus judgment without reading source code.
146	
147	Adopt this core only if it passes these checks with less conceptual machinery than repairing the current one. Do not build both as permanent product engines.
148	
149	**Review verification:** independently enumerating all sixteen joint states reproduced the four B probabilities `0.35`, `0.545`, `0.245`, and `0.325`, with total mass one to floating-point tolerance. The three sensitivity calculations also match. This verifies the illustration's arithmetic, not its invented inputs.

# A small quantitative alternative, worked end to end

**Status:** design experiment proposed for review; no product code changed. Every number below is invented for arithmetic demonstration, not a Hormuz forecast, a researched parameter, or a real market quote. Decimal precision is retained to let a reviewer reproduce the arithmetic; the product can round its display.

## What this experiment should settle

Can a small explicit causal model demonstrate the assignment's two use cases, immediate branching, and a financially meaningful thesis more clearly than the current temporal simulator?

The candidate uses four binary variables with fixed meanings. It has no sampled parameter distribution, daily noise process, implicit expiry of an assumption, or multiplied path score. It remains a **subjective causal hypothesis**. Correct arithmetic does not validate its assumptions.

## Define the claims and the relationships

| Variable | Claim | Role |
|---|---|---|
| H | The strait reopens on Monday under the chosen transit criterion | Historical event within the scenario |
| S | A specified military strike occurs on Tuesday | Additional event |
| F | Effective shipping flow exceeds the chosen threshold at the end of the first week | Continuing state, assessed at a date |
| B | The named Brent benchmark closes below the chosen threshold at the end of the second week | Financial outcome |

Proposed graph: `H → F ← S`, then `F → B`.

The mechanism hypothesis is that reopening enables flow recovery, a strike can hinder it, and recovered flow makes a lower price more likely. This is intentionally incomplete: demand, inventories, supply policy, and risk premia are held in background assumptions. If a strike affects price through an additional risk-premium channel, add `S → B` and the corresponding conditional table; do not pretend the flow channel captures it. If the chance of a strike depends on reopening, model that dependency instead of assuming independence.

For this arithmetic example only, H and S are independent roots with `P(H)=0.35` and `P(S)=0.20`. That independence is an assumption to challenge, not a property of geopolitical events.

## Write the local assumptions explicitly

The flow table means the chance that F is true for each combination of its two parents:

| H: reopened | S: strike | P(F=true given H,S) |
|---|---|---:|
| false | false | 0.10 |
| false | true | 0.05 |
| true | false | 0.80 |
| true | true | 0.25 |

The last row is the assignment's important interaction. Reopening and then suffering a strike is not the same scenario as reopening with no strike. No additive-strength approximation is required to express that distinction.

The financial table is `P(B=true | F=false)=0.20` and `P(B=true | F=true)=0.70`. These are subjective conditional probabilities under the proposed model. Interpreting them causally requires the stated parent structure to be adequate for the intended intervention; an observational table alone does not supply that warrant.

The joint probability assigned to one complete state is:

`P(H=h,S=s,F=f,B=b) = P(H=h) × P(S=s) × P(F=f | H=h,S=s) × P(B=b | F=f)`.

There are only sixteen complete states. Summing their probabilities computes the requested outcome without simulation error. This is the standard factorization of a Bayesian network; the causal interpretation is the additional modeling assumption. [CMU course notes](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15281/coursenotes/bayesnets/).

## Explore, then change one event

In the opening scenario, the user supposes H is true. The model replaces H's root distribution with that fixed value, leaving the remaining mechanisms unchanged. It does not claim the user can physically control the strait. This is a hypothetical intervention under a declared model. [Pearl, intervention semantics](https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/BOOK-2K/ch3-3.pdf).

Then:

`P(F | do(H=true)) = 0.80 × 0.80 + 0.20 × 0.25 = 0.69`.

`P(B | do(H=true)) = 0.69 × 0.70 + 0.31 × 0.20 = 0.545`.

Now create a branch supposing S is also true:

`P(F | do(H=true), do(S=true)) = 0.25`.

`P(B | do(H=true), do(S=true)) = 0.25 × 0.70 + 0.75 × 0.20 = 0.325`.

The branch lowers the model-implied chance of B by **22 percentage points**. The difference is explained by two named local tables. Monday's reopening remains true; Tuesday's strike changes the chance of Friday's flow recovery. No historical event has to be retracted.

The UI can say:

> Under these assumptions, a strike after reopening lowers the chance of the Brent threshold being met from 55% to 33%. The change runs through reduced shipping recovery. A direct effect on the risk premium is not modeled.

The mechanism's source appears separately from the table's owner and rationale. A source documenting the importance of shipping does not certify the numbers 0.80 or 0.25.

## Verify without a path product

To test whether reopening helps reach B, compare the defined intervention with its explicit alternative:

`P(F | do(H=false)) = 0.80 × 0.10 + 0.20 × 0.05 = 0.09`.

`P(B | do(H=false)) = 0.09 × 0.70 + 0.91 × 0.20 = 0.245`.

The modeled difference between reopening and not reopening is `0.545 − 0.245 = 0.30`. This answers a precise question under assumptions. It does not show that reopening alone is sufficient for B, prove the graph true, or establish a trade's profitability. “No reopening” can bundle physically different situations; the real-world interpretation is only as well-defined as this binary scenario distinction.

A useful Verify verdict is therefore:

> This model supports a downward-price mechanism, conditional on shipping recovery. The conclusion weakens substantially under renewed strikes. It remains sensitive to omitted demand and risk-premium mechanisms.

A graph search that finds no supported route should report its scope: “No supported chain found within this map and search budget.” It should not claim no causal relationship can exist.

## Turn the scenario into a financially valid question

Suppose, for illustration, that a matching binary contract pays $1 when B is true and $0 otherwise. A hypothetical executable YES ask is $0.40 and per-unit costs are $0.02.

Before H happens, the model's **unconditional** probability is calculated below. Here H has no parents, and the declared model makes `P(B | H)` equal to `P(B | do(H))`. That equality must not be assumed in an arbitrary causal graph.

`P(B) = 0.35 × 0.545 + 0.65 × 0.245 = 0.35`.

The expected unit payout is $0.35. For a position held to resolution, expected net profit per unit is:

`0.35 − 0.40 − 0.02 = −$0.07`.

Subtracting the current quote from the opening-scenario probability would instead suggest `0.545 − 0.40 − 0.02 = +$0.125`. That calculation answers a different question: a trade evaluated as though the opening were already given at an unchanged purchase price. It is not the pre-event expected payoff.

The honest conclusion is **no positive expected profit at this entry price under this model**. With these flat costs, the break-even probability is `0.40 + 0.02 = 0.42`; at a probability of 0.35, the break-even maximum ask is `$0.35 − $0.02 = $0.33`. Fees that depend on price or winnings require their actual formula. Alternatively, the user can define an entry rule after observing reopening, but the product must then use the quote available at that entry time. It cannot assume the old quote survives the news. This illustration omits quote movement before fill, settlement/counterparty risk, and capital/opportunity cost; it is not an executable trade assessment.

For ordinary assets, replace the binary payout with an explicit scenario price and a specified position. A probability of crossing a threshold does not define returns within each outcome, margin needs, maximum drawdown, or a probability of ruin. Leave those outputs absent until their required inputs exist.

## Represent uncertainty without manufacturing a distribution

Add named alternative assumptions only where they matter. For example:

| Assumption set | P(F | H=true,S=false) | P(F | H=true,S=true) | P(B | do(H=true)) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fragile recovery | 0.60 | 0.10 | 0.45 |
| Central illustration | 0.80 | 0.25 | 0.545 |
| Resilient recovery | 0.90 | 0.40 | 0.60 |

Other inputs remain fixed for this exercise. The 45–60% span is an **envelope over three tested assumptions**, not an 80% probability interval, not a bound over all plausible models, and not evidence that the true probability lies inside it. Adding the direct risk-premium channel would be a structural sensitivity case.

Do not blindly combine all low inputs for a low case and all high inputs for a high case. Negative effects and interactions can make that ordering wrong. Evaluate each specified case and report what was actually tested.

This lets a user ask “does my decision survive these alternatives?” without pretending the application knows a probability distribution over all its own errors.

## Smallest implementation boundary

- Keep the existing immutable graph, branch history, Inspector, source records, generated browser types, and keyless replay idea.
- A numerical claim carries its parent set, a complete local conditional table, and a parameter owner/rationale. A claim may remain unquantified.
- A model defines a bounded collection of dated binary claims. Numerical dependencies must be closed: an unknown input prevents that output from being calculated.
- For a small cap, compute by exact enumeration. Count nodes after any explicit time expansion. If the cap is exceeded, decline the numerical calculation or ask for a smaller focus; do not silently switch semantics.
- A scenario edit fixes a specific dated claim. Distinguish this from learning that it occurred. An observation query can be added by exact conditioning once its interface and tests are ready.
- Conditional tables do not identify individual-level counterfactuals. Do not claim to know what the same realized world would have done differently without a structural model of its shared disturbances.
- Keep named sensitivity cases as complete explicit model variants. Do not turn their counts into probabilities or average them without a justified weighting rule.
- Store the model/schema version and the branch in the exported thesis. A later mathematical change should not silently rewrite the meaning of an older artifact.

This is a candidate to test, not a demand for a framework supporting every model class. The main tradeoff is elicitation burden: four understandable numbers can be better than two obscure log-odds pushes, but they remain four unsupported numbers if nobody can defend them. If the example cannot justify its parameters, keep the mechanism and show scenario consequences without a numeric probability. That is a valid result of the design experiment.

## Acceptance tests before adoption

1. Reproduce every calculation above with an independent small enumerator or hand oracle.
2. Verify total probability is one and impossible events remain zero.
3. In a shared-cause example, distinguish observing an event from intervening on it; reproduce Bayes' rule numerically.
4. In an interaction table, preserve the joint-parent row rather than synthesizing it from independent pushes.
5. Changing a root assumption leaves unrelated claims unchanged.
6. Monday's reopening and Tuesday's strike can both occur without contradiction.
7. A missing conditional row or an unquantified parent yields an explicit incomplete result.
8. Export the exact branch and assumption set currently displayed.
9. Use the unconditional belief for a pre-event binary expected-payoff calculation; use a post-event quote for a post-event entry rule.
10. Have a reviewer explain the before/after thesis and identify which inputs are evidence versus judgment without reading source code.

Adopt this core only if it passes these checks with less conceptual machinery than repairing the current one. Do not build both as permanent product engines.

**Review verification:** independently enumerating all sixteen joint states reproduced the four B probabilities `0.35`, `0.545`, `0.245`, and `0.325`, with total mass one to floating-point tolerance. The three sensitivity calculations also match. This verifies the illustration's arithmetic, not its invented inputs.

1	# Independent finance review
2	
3	**First-pass freeze:** 2026-09-21. This review was written from `ASSIGNMENT.md` and `AGENTS.md` only. I did not inspect the product requirements, architecture, specifications, decision records, brainstorming, code, prior research, or other plans before freezing it.
4	
5	## Recommendation
6	
7	Build a small **scenario workbench** that turns an event hypothesis into an auditable path from event, through real-world mechanisms, to a trade. Its most important job is to prevent a financially dangerous shortcut:
8	
9	> Event true does not imply price up or price down.
10	
11	Prices respond to information relative to what was already expected, and also to changes in risk premia, liquidity, positioning, timing, and the chosen instrument. Kuttner's event study is a clean empirical example: anticipated policy changes had essentially no effect on bond rates, while unanticipated changes had large effects ([Federal Reserve Bank of New York](https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/staff_reports/sr99.html)).
12	
13	The prototype should therefore keep five things separate:
14	
15	1. **What happens:** a resolvable event or state of the world.
16	2. **Why it matters:** a causal mechanism with conditions and a time lag.
17	3. **What the market expected:** the priced baseline at a stated time.
18	4. **What can be traded:** a specific instrument with expiry, basis, liquidity, and costs.
19	5. **What happens along the way:** a price path that can trigger exits before the terminal view is right.
20	
21	This separation is more useful than a large graph with invented probabilities. A polished, seeded example plus editable assumptions would demonstrate the concept better than a broad but unauditable “quant platform.”
22	
23	## The minimum useful experience
24	
25	### 1. Turn the input into a testable event
26	
27	The input “The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week” is incomplete. Before drawing a graph, the tool should expose a compact event contract:
28	
29	- **Claim:** what observable condition counts as open?
30	- **Deadline:** by what time, in what time zone?
31	- **Measure:** unrestricted vessel passage, oil flow, or an official declaration?
32	- **Threshold:** any traffic, normal traffic, or a stated volume?
33	- **Observation source:** who settles whether it happened?
34	- **As-of time:** when were the market and evidence snapshots taken?
35	
36	The tool can propose these fields, but uncertainty must remain visible until the user accepts them. Without them, branches cannot be compared or scored later.
37	
38	### 2. Draw a mechanism map, not a story chain
39	
40	Use a directed graph, but keep the first graph deliberately small: about 6–10 nodes and 8–14 links. Every link should answer a full sentence:
41	
42	> If the source changes, the destination changes in this direction, after this lag, provided these conditions hold, because this mechanism applies.
43	
44	Each link needs:
45	
46	- direction and expected sign;
47	- earliest and typical lag;
48	- conditions that must remain true;
49	- an impact range, or “direction only” when magnitude is unsupported;
50	- evidence for the mechanism, magnitude, and timing;
51	- counterevidence or a named failure mode;
52	- provenance: user judgment, model proposal, market observation, or cited source;
53	- confidence owned by the party making the judgment.
54	
55	The graph is a structured set of assumptions. It does not prove causation. Pearl's original treatment describes causal diagrams as a language for combining statistical and subject-matter assumptions, and as a way to identify what further observations would be needed ([Pearl, 1995](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6gv9n38c)).
56	
57	A plausible Hormuz path is:
58	
59	`shipping access -> effective export capacity -> seaborne supply -> inventory expectations -> prompt physical balance -> Brent curve and price`
60	
61	Important modifiers belong as explicit parents, not footnotes: OPEC+ output choices, damaged infrastructure, tanker insurance, sanctions enforcement, demand, inventories, spare pipeline capacity, and renewed attack risk. The EIA's chokepoint analysis is a good example of mechanism evidence: it separately reports flows and bypass capacity rather than treating “open” as a binary supply switch ([U.S. EIA](https://www.eia.gov/international/content/analysis/special_topics/World_Oil_Transit_Chokepoints/)).
62	
63	### 3. Put the priced baseline beside the causal map
64	
65	For every tradable outcome, show three separate judgments:
66	
67	| Judgment | Example | Meaning |
68	|---|---|---|
69	| Event belief | “70% open by Friday” | User or model forecast of event truth |
70	| Market baseline | “Options and curve imply substantial disruption risk” | What appears priced at the as-of time |
71	| Conditional move | “If normal flows resume and no attack occurs, Brent is 4–9% lower after five sessions” | Scenario payoff, not event probability |
72	
73	The price effect is the difference between the market's prior distribution and its updated distribution, not the event label alone. Event studies formalize this as an **abnormal return** around new information ([MacKinlay, 1997](https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/jeclit/v35y1997i1p13-39.html)).
74	
75	Market-implied probabilities also need a label rather than being presented as ground truth. Prediction-market prices can often be close to mean beliefs under particular assumptions, but the mapping depends on traders' beliefs and preferences ([Wolfers and Zitzewitz, 2006](https://www.nber.org/papers/w12200)). Options encode state prices and risk preferences, not a clean physical probability by default.
76	
77	### 4. Branch by intervention and compare only descendants
78	
79	Clicking a node should offer “hold this outcome fixed and branch.” The alternate world preserves ancestors and unrelated nodes, then recomputes only descendants. The comparison should show:
80	
81	- assumptions added, removed, or changed;
82	- links whose conditions fail;
83	- timing shifts;
84	- resulting instrument payoff ranges;
85	- new evidence needed to distinguish the worlds.
86	
87	Useful branch types are:
88	
89	- **Baseline:** the user's current best view.
90	- **Alternative:** a plausible competing outcome.
91	- **Stress:** a severe but coherent path; likelihood may be intentionally unspecified.
92	- **Reverse stress:** begin with an unacceptable loss and ask which combinations of events could produce it.
93	
94	Do not force these branches to sum to 100%. They may overlap and they may omit possibilities. Expected profit and loss is valid only if the scenarios are mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive, assigned coherent probabilities, valued at the same horizon, and net of costs. Under those conditions:
95	
96	`expected P&L = sum of (scenario probability × scenario P&L) − trading costs`
97	
98	Do not multiply link confidence scores to manufacture a path probability. That is valid only when each number is a conditional probability given all relevant parents and the dependencies are modeled correctly. A confidence label about evidence quality is not a probability.
99	
100	### 5. Make time a first-class part of the answer
101	
102	One target-price node hides the most useful information. Keep these clocks separate:
103	
104	- event deadline;
105	- mechanism lag on each link;
106	- forecast horizon for each price estimate;
107	- intended holding period;
108	- instrument expiry or roll date;
109	- monitoring frequency and exit trigger.
110	
111	Show a few decision-relevant checkpoints, for example announcement, one session, five sessions, and one month. A market can rally before an expected opening, fall on confirmation, and rise a day later after a new attack. All three moves can be consistent with the same physical mechanism.
112	
113	## The final tradable thesis
114	
115	The last screen should be an editable trade card, not a prose summary. It should contain:
116	
117	| Field | Required content |
118	|---|---|
119	| Thesis | One sentence linking surprise, mechanism, and instrument |
120	| Instrument | Exact asset or contract, venue, expiry, and quote convention |
121	| Direction | Long, short, spread, or hedge |
122	| Entry | Price or observable event condition and valid window |
123	| Priced baseline | Market observation and as-of time |
124	| Edge | User belief or impact range minus the priced baseline |
125	| Catalysts | Observable milestones and expected dates |
126	| Invalidation | Which causal observation would make the thesis wrong |
127	| Exit | Time exit, thesis exit, take-profit, and any stop instruction |
128	| Scenario payoff | P&L range under each named branch, including costs |
129	| Loss boundary | Maximum acceptable loss under stated assumptions |
130	| Execution risks | Liquidity, gap, basis, expiry, carry, borrow, and slippage |
131	| Evidence | Sources attached to the specific claims they support |
132	
133	A useful one-line thesis would read:
134	
135	> If sustained vessel flow recovers faster than the oil curve currently discounts, and export infrastructure remains operational, short the named Brent contract through the five-session normalization window; exit if flow recovery stalls below the accepted threshold or conflict risk re-escalates.
136	
137	The contract matters. A correct view on physical oil can still lose in the selected futures month because of basis or curve changes. The CFTC defines basis risk as an unexpected widening or narrowing between the exposure and the futures hedge ([CFTC glossary](https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm)). An option can lose despite a correct directional view because expiry, implied volatility, and path also matter.
138	
139	The prototype should stop at a decision-ready draft. Position sizing can be a simple user-entered loss budget. 144	
145	Two scenarios can end at the same price and produce different realized P&L:
146

153

156	- **stop order:** an execution instruction that may fill away from its trigger;

Expected shortfall is the average of losses beyond that cutoff ([Basel Committee standard](https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d457.pdf)).

165	Stress tests answer a different question: what happens under a named severe path? 168

170	- worst loss among the scenarios explored;
171	- assumptions and risks omitted from every scenario;
172	- no “VaR” label.
173	
174	### Unknown black swans cannot be enumerated

179

181	2. **Sensitivity:** which single assumption or link changes the trade most?

187	
188	Evidence belongs on claims and links, not in a bibliography detached from the graph. Each citation should record title, publisher, date, URL, access time, and the exact claim it supports. Separate four jobs:
189	
190	- **Existence:** does the event or exposure exist?
191	- **Mechanism:** can the source plausibly affect the destination?
192	- **Magnitude:** how large was or could the effect be?

201	1. **True event, opposite price move.** Hormuz opens, but oil rises because opening was fully priced and an unexpected strike raises the chance of a longer disruption.
202	2. **Correct mechanism, wrong instrument.** Gulf exports normalize, but a WTI contract underperforms the expected Brent move because location and curve basis change.

214	These are **engineering estimates**, not observations from the existing codebase.
